title: The Design of Everyday Cryptography
excerpt: Cryptography Should Be Hard to Use Improperly
content_html:
Cryptographers (and Applied Cryptographers) love to define beautiful, robust, complete protocols that solve interesting problems. And if you get enough Cryptographers (or Applied Cryptographers) into the room, they are gonna define protocols that solve a lot of interesting problems.

And if we’re lucky, at least some of those interesting problems will matter to the security of a system someday.

Unfortunately, any cryptographic protocol that solves sufficiently many sufficiently interesting problems will be impossible for mere mortals to use safely. It will be the Norman Door of cryptographic protocols.

KEMs

A nice example of an easy-to-use cryptographic interface is the KEM, or Key Encapsulation Mechanism.

My favorite diagram of a KEM is from FIPS 203, above. We can also express the KEM interface as code:

def kem_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (public_key, private_key)

def kem_encaps(pub: PublicKey) -> tuple[SharedSecret, Ciphertext]:
  # Generate a random shared secret and the ciphertext that encapsulates it.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return (ss, ct)

def kem_decaps(priv: PrivateKey, ct: Ciphertext) -> SharedSecret:
  # Decapsulate the ciphertext to get the shared secret inside.
  ...
  return ss

As a prospective user of this interface, it’s easy enough for me to tell that I’m supposed to use kem_keygen to generate my key, and then I can use the public key with kem_encaps and the private key with kem_decaps. Inspecting the inputs to these functions, I’m faced with the following questions:

  • What kind of seed do I need?
  • Which parms should I use?
  • What should I do with my SharedSecret?

For a given algorithm (e.g., ML-KEM) the first two are questions with few answers. ML-KEM, for example, takes a 64-byte seed d || z and there are 3 parameter sets targeting different security strengths.

The third question is not supposed to be answered by your KEM, but by your symmetric crypto primitive (not pictured).

Note that I don’t have to choose any inputs to kem_encaps or kem_decaps. Those functions only take things that were provided to me by the other functions. For folks familiar with RSA encryption or IES, it might be a bit of a culture shock that you don’t get to decide what gets encrypted. But this is liberating. You don’t have to worry about what happens if you encrypt a low-entropy value because you don’t get to pick the value at all. Instead, you are given a SharedSecret to plug into your authenticated encryption primitive of choice.

Also note that every input and output is of a type with some bounded maximum size (e.g., the maximum size of PublicKey for ML-KEM is 1568).

Seems pretty easy. Let’s look at a less-nice situation: modern digital signatures.

Signatures

The big snake pit you have to jump over when trying to use a modern digital signature is pre-hashing.

Prehashing is a very strange topic. Half of the cryptographic community insists that it’s absolutely essential, while the other half has never heard of it. Usually the half that has never heard of it is theoretical cryptographers.

— Sophie Schmieg

For even more wisdom: see Sophie’s excellent write-up “HashML-DSA considered harmful”.

The prehashing question becomes additional variety (in the cybernetics sense) that must be handled by additional variety at the interface level.

We can create pure and prehash variants of the sign and verify functions.

def dsa_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (pub, priv)

def dsa_sign_pure(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes, msg: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the pure signature over the context and message using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_sign_prehash(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes, hash_alg: HashAlgorithm, hash: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the prehash signature over the context and hash using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes, msg: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the pure signature over the context and message using the key.
  ...
  return ok

def dsa_verify_prehash(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes, hash_alg: HashAlgorithm, hash: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the prehash signature over the context and hash using the key.
  ...
  return ok

I almost forgot about the “External Mu” trick (e.g., FIPS 204, Algorithm 7, Line 6) which is equivalent to pure signing, but allows computing the fixed-length message representative hash (which includes ctx) before passing it to the signer, which helps with the problem below. Let’s add it…

def dsa_sign_pure_mu(priv: PrivateKey, mu: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the signature over the mu value using the key.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure_mu(priv: PrivateKey, mu: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the signature over the mu value using the key.
  ...
  return sig

Unlike the KEM case, the inputs these functions are not fixed-length. msg might be 100 bytes or 100 gigabytes. This creates obvious problems for embedded cryptographic interfaces, like hardware tokens or TPMs, which tend to have limits on the maximum size of requests or responses. Pre-hashing was supposed to help with this, but since HashML-DSA and HashSLH-DSA are different algorithms to ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, it doesn’t help much, since embedded crypto people understand that we will be asked to support the same protocols as everybody else, and “just totally modify your protocol to use a different cryptographic algorithm” is not a great answer.

So, we have to implement start/update/finish APIs (like those used for hashing):

def dsa_sign_pure_start(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes) -> SignatureSequence:
  # Starts a signature with the given key and context.
  ...
  return seq

def dsa_sign_pure_update(seq: SignatureSequence, data: bytes):
  # Adds the given data into the signature.
  ...

def dsa_sign_pure_complete(seq: SignatureSequence) -> Signature:
  # Finishes producing the signature.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure_start(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes) -> VerifySequence:
  # Starts verifying a signature with the given key and context.
  ...
  return seq

def dsa_verify_pure_update(seq: VerifySequence, data: bytes):
  # Adds the given data into the signature.
  ...

def dsa_verify_pure_complete(seq: VerifySequence, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Finishes checking the signature.
  ...
  return ok

Yikes. So unlike for KEMs, where we had 3 APIs and 2 input decisions, we have 13 APIs and the following 5 decisions:

  • (Same as KEM) What kind of seed do I need?
  • (Same as KEM) Which parms should I use?
  • Should I use pure or prehash?
  • (If using prehash) Which hash algorithm should I use?
  • What do I put into ctx?

All this variety was introduced on purpose in order to provide some (real or perceived) security benefit:

  • Pure signatures allow the security of the signature not to depend on the collision resistance of the chosen hash algorithm (second preimage resistance is still required, though)
  • The ctx (context string) pulls domain separation (e.g., if one key signs two different types of messages) into the signature itself (instead of in the higher-level protocol that uses the signature)

Why are KEMs so simple and signatures so complex? One reason is that the Key Encapsulation Mechanism has a really nice indirection in the SharedSecret. It isn’t the KEM’s business what you do with that secret. Do some symmetric crypto with it. It doesn’t care. Your actual data that you want to encrypt is none of your KEM’s business.

Modern digital signatures are comparatively micro-managers. The actual data that you want to sign is still your signature’s business.

Making Signatures More Usable

What could help here? I’m a software engineer so I am obligated to suggest: maybe another indirection?

Imagine if signatures were defined over fixed-size message representatives:

def dsa_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (pub, priv)

def dsa_sign_mrep(priv: PrivateKey, mrep: MessageRepresentative) -> Signature:
  # Computes the signature over the message representative using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_mrep(pub: PublicKey, mrep: MessageRepresentative, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the signature over the message representative using the key.
  ...
  return ok

The actual length of the MessageRepresentative would depend on the signing primitive (e.g., 64 bytes for ML-DSA, 32 bytes for ECDSA-P256, 256 bytes for RSA-2048).

A separate cryptographic protocol could define what to feed into a XOF (such as SHAKE256) to compute mrep:

  • Incorporating a unique prefix that identifies the mrep scheme itself
  • Incorporating an optional context string
  • Incorporating a public key hash (to provide e.g., Beyond Unforgeability properties on signatures that weren’t designed with those properties in mind)
  • Incorporating randomness for hedging (against e.g., side-channel risks)

General Principles

Signatures won’t be re-designed based on a random blog post from some crank on the internet (well, not this crank at least). But hopefully the above discussion on signatures helps illustrate some principles that can be followed in the design of cryptographic interfaces of all levels (from primitives fo higher-level protocols:

Protocols should be opinionated

Do not provide unnecessary knobs to the user. Users will turn them and find ways to harm themselves. How do you know if a knob is necessary?

  • Necessary: Two different realistic threat models justify the two different values.
  • Unnecessary: It would be fun to be able to change this value.

Protocols should have one job

Follow the Single Responsibility Principle. A protocol doesn’t need to do everything. Make composable systems of small, single-purpose protocols (e.g., KEM + Authenticated Encryption).

Protocols should be known-answer-testable

Cryptographic protocols are easy to get wrong (or worse, slightly wrong). Make it easy to test an implementation using test vectors (these inputs -> those outputs).

Protocols should be upgradeable

No matter how carefully a protocol is designed, it will need to be updated later. Whether because of a serious flaw or just a new optimization or use case, you will need to be able to change things. Think about what will happen when two parties that support different versions of the protocol try to talk to each other.

content_html_zh:
密码学家（和应用密码学家）喜欢定义漂亮、健壮、完整的协议来解决有趣的问题。 如果你有足够多的密码学家（或应用密码学家）进入房间，他们将定义解决许多有趣问题的协议。

如果我们幸运的话，至少其中一些有趣的问题有一天会对系统的安全产生影响。

不幸的是，任何能够解决足够多足够有趣的问题的加密协议对于普通人来说都是不可能安全使用的。 它将成为密码协议的诺曼门。

KEMs

易于使用的加密接口的一个很好的例子是 KEM（密钥封装机制）。

我最喜欢的 KEM 图来自上面的 FIPS 203。 我们还可以将 KEM 接口表示为代码：

def kem_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (public_key, private_key)

def kem_encaps(pub: PublicKey) -> tuple[SharedSecret, Ciphertext]:
  # Generate a random shared secret and the ciphertext that encapsulates it.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return (ss, ct)

def kem_decaps(priv: PrivateKey, ct: Ciphertext) -> SharedSecret:
  # Decapsulate the ciphertext to get the shared secret inside.
  ...
  return ss

作为该界面的潜在用户，我很容易就知道我应该使用 kem_keygen 来生成我的密钥，然后我可以将公钥与 kem_encaps 一起使用，将私钥与 kem_decaps 一起使用。 检查这些函数的输入时，我面临以下问题：

  • 我需要什么样的种子？
  • 我应该使用哪些参数？
  • 我应该如何处理我的 SharedSecret？

对于给定的算法（例如 ML-KEM），前两个问题的答案很少。 例如，ML-KEM 采用 64 字节种子 d || z 并且有 3 个针对不同安全强度的参数集。

第三个问题不应该由您的 KEM 来回答，而是由您的对称加密原语（未显示）来回答。

请注意，我不必为 kem_encaps 或 kem_decaps 选择任何输入。 这些函数只接受其他函数提供给我的东西。 对于熟悉 RSA 加密或 IES 的人来说，您无法决定加密的内容可能会有点文化冲击。 但这是一种解放。 您不必担心加密低熵值会发生什么，因为您根本无法选择该值。 相反，您将获得一个 SharedSecret 来插入您选择的经过身份验证的加密原语。

另请注意，每个输入和输出的类型都有一定的最大大小（例如，ML-KEM 的 PublicKey 的最大大小为 1568）。

看起来很容易。 让我们看看一个不太好的情况：现代数字签名。

签名

当尝试使用现代数字签名时，你必须跳过的大蛇坑是预哈希。

预哈希是一个非常奇怪的话题。 密码学界的一半人坚持认为它绝对必要，而另一半人则从未听说过它。 通常，从未听说过它的一半是理论密码学家。

— 索菲·施米格

如需更多智慧：请参阅 Sophie 的精彩文章“HashML-DSA 被认为是有害的”。

预哈希问题变成了额外的多样性（在控制论意义上），必须通过接口级别的额外多样性来处理。

我们可以创建签名和验证函数的纯变体和预哈希变体。

def dsa_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (pub, priv)

def dsa_sign_pure(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes, msg: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the pure signature over the context and message using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_sign_prehash(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes, hash_alg: HashAlgorithm, hash: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the prehash signature over the context and hash using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes, msg: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the pure signature over the context and message using the key.
  ...
  return ok

def dsa_verify_prehash(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes, hash_alg: HashAlgorithm, hash: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the prehash signature over the context and hash using the key.
  ...
  return ok

我几乎忘记了“外部 Mu”技巧（例如，FIPS 204，算法 7，第 6 行），它相当于纯签名，但允许在将其传递给签名者之前计算固定长度消息代表哈希（包括 ctx），这有助于解决下面的问题。 让我们添加它...

def dsa_sign_pure_mu(priv: PrivateKey, mu: bytes) -> Signature:
  # Computes the signature over the mu value using the key.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure_mu(priv: PrivateKey, mu: bytes, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the signature over the mu value using the key.
  ...
  return sig

与 KEM 情况不同，这些函数的输入不是固定长度的。 msg 可能是 100 字节或 100 GB。 这给嵌入式加密接口（如硬件令牌或 TPM）带来了明显的问题，它们往往对请求或响应的最大大小有限制。 预哈希应该对此有所帮助，但由于 HashML-DSA 和 HashSLH-DSA 与 ML-DSA 和 SLH-DSA 是不同的算法，因此它没有多大帮助，因为嵌入式加密人们知道我们将被要求支持与其他人相同的协议，并且“只是完全修改您的协议以使用不同的加密算法”并不是一个很好的答案。

因此，我们必须实现开始/更新/完成 API（如用于散列的 API）：

def dsa_sign_pure_start(priv: PrivateKey, ctx: bytes) -> SignatureSequence:
  # Starts a signature with the given key and context.
  ...
  return seq

def dsa_sign_pure_update(seq: SignatureSequence, data: bytes):
  # Adds the given data into the signature.
  ...

def dsa_sign_pure_complete(seq: SignatureSequence) -> Signature:
  # Finishes producing the signature.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_pure_start(pub: PublicKey, ctx: bytes) -> VerifySequence:
  # Starts verifying a signature with the given key and context.
  ...
  return seq

def dsa_verify_pure_update(seq: VerifySequence, data: bytes):
  # Adds the given data into the signature.
  ...

def dsa_verify_pure_complete(seq: VerifySequence, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Finishes checking the signature.
  ...
  return ok

哎呀。 因此，与 KEM 不同的是，我们有 3 个 API 和 2 个输入决策，而我们有 13 个 API 和以下 5 个决策：

  • （与KEM相同）我需要什么样的种子？
  • （与 KEM 相同）我应该使用哪些参数？
  • 我应该使用纯还是预哈希？
  • （如果使用预哈希）我应该使用哪种哈希算法？
  • 我要在 ctx 中放入什么？

所有这些多样性都是有意引入的，以便提供一些（真实的或感知的）安全优势：

  • 纯签名允许签名的安全性不依赖于所选哈希算法的抗冲突性（尽管仍然需要第二个原像抗性）
  • ctx（上下文字符串）将域分离（例如，如果一个密钥签署两种不同类型的消息）拉入签名本身（而不是在使用签名的更高级别协议中）

为什么 KEM 如此简单而签名如此复杂？ 原因之一是密钥封装机制在 SharedSecret 中具有非常好的间接性。 你如何处理这个秘密与 KEM 无关。 用它做一些对称加密。 它不在乎。 您想要加密的实际数据与您的 KEM 无关。

现代数字签名是相对微观的管理者。 您想要签名的实际数据仍然是您签名的事。

让签名更有用

这里有什么可以帮助的？ 我是一名软件工程师，所以我有义务建议：也许还有另一种间接方式？

想象一下，如果签名是通过固定大小的消息代表来定义的：

def dsa_keygen(seed: bytes, parms: ParameterSet) -> tuple[PublicKey, PrivateKey]:
  # Use eldritch algebra to expand the given random seed into an actual keypair.
  ...
  return (pub, priv)

def dsa_sign_mrep(priv: PrivateKey, mrep: MessageRepresentative) -> Signature:
  # Computes the signature over the message representative using the key.
  # Optionally, a test-only "derandomized" version of this function might exist,
  # e.g., for Wycheproof test cases.
  ...
  return sig

def dsa_verify_mrep(pub: PublicKey, mrep: MessageRepresentative, sig: Signature) -> bool:
  # Verifies the signature over the message representative using the key.
  ...
  return ok

MessageRepresentative 的实际长度取决于签名原语（例如，ML-DSA 为 64 字节，ECDSA-P256 为 32 字节，RSA-2048 为 256 字节）。

单独的加密协议可以定义输入 XOF（例如 SHAKE256）的内容来计算 mrep：

  • 合并一个唯一的前缀来标识 mrep 方案本身
  • 合并可选的上下文字符串
  • 合并公钥哈希（例如，为签名提供超越不可伪造性属性，而这些签名在设计时并未考虑到这些属性）
  • 纳入对冲的随机性（例如，针对侧通道风险）

一般原则

签名不会根据互联网上某个怪人的随机博客文章重新设计（好吧，至少不是这个怪人）。 但希望上述关于签名的讨论有助于说明在设计所有级别的加密接口时可以遵循的一些原则（从更高级别协议的原语：

协议应该有主见

不要向用户提供不必要的旋钮。 用户会转向它们并找到伤害自己的方法。 您如何知道是否需要旋钮？

  • 必要性：两种不同的现实威胁模型证明了两种不同的价值。
  • 不必要：能够改变这个值会很有趣。

协议应该有一份工作

遵循单一职责原则。 协议不需要做所有事情。 制作小型、单一用途协议的可组合系统（例如 KEM + 身份验证加密）。

协议应该是已知的、答案可测试的

加密协议很容易出错（或者更糟糕的是，稍微出错）。 使用测试向量（这些输入 -> 那些输出）可以轻松测试实现。

协议应该是可升级的

无论协议设计得多么仔细，以后都需要更新。 无论是因为严重缺陷还是只是新的优化或用例，您都需要能够进行更改。 想象一下当支持不同版本协议的两方尝试相互对话时会发生什么。
